analysis.one_liner: Bans golden parachute payouts to Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac executives unless Congress names them in law.
analysis.headline: No one co-sponsored the bill and the Financial Services Committee never took it up; it died there when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: In September 2008, days after the federal government took control of Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, Rep. Peter Welch proposed barring severance or 'golden parachute' payments to the executives and board members of the two mortgage-finance giants. Under his bill, the Treasury-backed companies could not pay an executive a golden parachute unless a federal law was passed that named that specific person and identified the payment. The bill died in committee without a hearing, a vote, or a single co-sponsor.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers, who had just absorbed responsibility for the two companies' trillion-dollar mortgage portfolios and their mounting losses. The bill would have made sure departing executives and directors could not collect large exit payments without Congress voting to approve each payment by name.

how_it_helps.text: The bill added a new paragraph to the Federal Housing Enterprises Financial Safety and Soundness Act of 1992 stating that no golden parachute or indemnification payment may be made to any executive officer or board member of Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac, except under a federal law that specifically names the individual and identifies the payment. [S3]

The CRS summary confirms the bill's purpose was to prohibit golden parachute and indemnification payments to Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac executives and directors unless Congress specifically authorized them by name. [S2]

analysis.who_pays: If it had passed, the cost would have fallen on Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac executives and board members, whose pre-negotiated exit packages could not be paid out unless Congress passed a law naming each recipient. The companies themselves would lose a lever for recruiting and retaining executives in the middle of a crisis.
analysis.who_pays_short: Fannie and Freddie executives and directors

drawbacks.text: The bill was introduced days after the government takeover, without a single co-sponsor, offering no evidence of support beyond its author; critics could view it as a symbolic gesture rather than a workable measure, since it would require Congress to pass a separate law naming each individual executive to authorize any exit payment. [S3] [S4]

The underlying statute the bill amended had just been enacted weeks earlier in the Federal Housing Finance Regulatory Reform Act of 2008, which had already placed restrictions on such payments; the bill tightened that restriction rather than addressing pay-setting from scratch, and a stricter payment ban in the middle of the conservatorship could complicate efforts to recruit or hold leadership at the troubled companies. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For ordinary taxpayers the benefit was straightforward: none of their money would fund executive exit packages without a named, recorded congressional approval. The cost — making it harder to compensate executives steering two failed companies through a crisis — was real but modest, and the existing law already restricted such payments. The bill's failure came from never getting any committee attention, not from a substantive objection on the record.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee on the day it was introduced and the committee never held a hearing, a markup, or a vote on it, so it simply expired when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009.

narrative.text: Rep. Peter Welch introduced the bill on September 15, 2008, and it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services that same day. [S5]
That was the only action ever taken: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote before the Congress ended. [S5]
No representative signed on as a co-sponsor, so the bill had the support of exactly one member of the 435-seat House. [S4]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac executives and directors are better off: the stricter ban never became law, and their severance and indemnification treatment continued under the compensation rules already in place after the government takeover.

for.name: Rep. Peter Welch
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to bar golden parachute payments to Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac executives and directors unless Congress authorized each payment by name.

against.name: Rep. Barney Frank
against.role: Chair, House Committee on Financial Services
against.what_they_did: The Financial Services Committee, which he chaired, received the bill by referral and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on it before the Congress ended.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.role: Committee of referral for housing-finance legislation
against.what_they_did: Held the bill without any recorded action — no hearing, no markup, no report — for the final three and a half months of the 110th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, and the bill had zero co-sponsors, so there is no record of how members of either party would have lined up. [S4] [S5]

industries.industry: Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac executives and directors
industries.note: The bill would have stripped their ability to collect golden parachute or indemnification payments from companies the federal government had just taken over, unless Congress approved each payment by name. Ordinary taxpayers were underwriting the two companies' losses, so executive exit payments came directly out of the public's rescue.

The bill did not change how the companies operated or lend; it only limited pay to their top officers and directors. A stricter pay ban could make it harder to recruit leadership mid-crisis, but the companies' core business was untouched.
